title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
On February 8th, 2026, the Seattle Seahawks and New England Patriots will face off in Super Bowl LX in New Orleans. This is the final showdown at the end of 32 teams battling it out across 17 weeks, and a gruelling playoffs where the most successful teams battle each other in a three-round, post-season elimination battle.
The two finalists were determined at the end of the NFC (National Football Conference) and AFC (American Football Conference) championship games, on Sunday 25th of January. The next 2 weeks to the final will lead to much speculation, but one question dominates the conversation: who will win? The conventional wisdom suggests that the teams in each conference are evenly matched, and this game will be decided on a coin-flip. Most expert panels are favouring Seattle to lift the Lombardi trophy. But what happens when we let the data speak for itself?
Using two distinct statistical approaches; a FiveThirtyEight-style Elo rating system, and a historical simulation model, I’ve analyzed the entire 2025 NFL season to predict not just the winner, but the final score, the likely performance metrics, and the underlying uncertainty in one of sport’s most-watched single games.
The verdict? This is not a coin flip. The models agree: Seattle has a clear advantage, with a ~60% win probability. But more interesting than the prediction itself is the journey to get there, and what it reveals about the limits of statistical forecasting in sports.






NotePrediction Accountability



These predictions were locked and published on February 7, 2026, before the game. All code and data are available on GitHub. This wasn’t written with the benefit of hindsight—it’s a genuine test of whether statistical models can outperform conventional wisdom.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
Why These Two Teams?
Before diving into statistics and prediction models, it’s worth stating that both Seattle and New England genuinely earned their way here. The design of the NFL schedule mean that teams play a broad cross-section of the league, and that no matter what injuries occur, what the weather on match-day is or any other bad luck that the teams might encounter, over the course of a season then things should balance out. Some fans have argued that the Denver Broncos losing their key playmaker, Quarterback Bo Nix, in the game before the AFC Championship has given the Patriots an easier journey to the Superbowl. However, the fact that these teams have reached the final is not a statistical fluke — they have been the two best teams in football throughout the 2025 season.

Figure 1: Offensive vs Defensive Performance - 2025 Season





Figure 1 shows where Seattle and New England sit relative to the entire league. Both teams occupy the upper-right, elite quadrant: high offensive output combined with iron-tight defense.

Figure 2: Performance Rankings - Top 10 Teams for different game elements Through 2025 Season





Figure 2 shows that both teams ranked highly in each aspect of performance, with both teams having a top 3 points scored per game of the regular season, and top 3 average points differential. Seattle ranked 1st in defense, having only allowed an average of 17.1 per game, and also the 3rd best offense, having averaged 29.2 points per game, giving them the league’s best point differential at +12.1. New England posted top-4 marks in both categories, with a +8.8 differential. These impressive statistics qualify both teams for the 1st and 2nd position for combined rankings.
This isn’t just about making the playoffs — it’s about sustained excellence across 17 regular season games and two/three playoff victories.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
The Models
I employed two fundamentally different approaches to prediction, each with distinct strengths and weaknesses.

1. Elo Rating System
The Elo model, adapted from FiveThirtyEight’s NFL methodology, treats team strength as a dynamic quantity that evolves game-by-game throughout the season.
Core principles:

Each team starts with a rating (1505 at the beginning of 2015)
Ratings increase after wins, decrease after losses
The magnitude of change depends on:

Margin of victory (blowouts matter more)
Opponent strength (beating good teams is more impressive)
Game importance (playoffs weighted more heavily)

Between seasons, ratings regress 1/3 toward the mean

Although it may seam counter-intuitive that all teams would have the same ranking at the beginning of the 2015 season, the beauty of the Elo model is that team rankings will be rewarded/penalised fairly quickly and that they will converge to their actual Elo rankings fairly quickly. There are parameters which determine how much teams get rewarded/penalised per victory/loss, as outlined below.
Key parameters:

K-factor (regular season): 20
K-factor (playoffs): 30
Home field advantage: 65 Elo points (~2.6 point spread)
Super Bowl: Neutral site (no home advantage)

For neutral-site games, Elo win probability follows the standard formula:
\[P(\text{Team A wins}) = \frac{1}{1 + 10^{(\text{Elo}_B - \text{Elo}_A)/400}}\]
After each game, Elo ratings are updated based on the result:
\[\Delta\text{Elo} = K \times \ln(|\text{game margin}| + 1) \times (1 - E)\]
where: - \(K\) is the K-factor (20 for regular season, 30 for playoffs) - \(\text{game margin}\) is the point difference (winner’s score - loser’s score) - \(E\) is the expected win probability of the victorious team before the game - \(\ln\) is the natural logarithm
The winner’s rating increases by \(\Delta\text{Elo}\), and the loser’s rating decreases by the same amount:
\[\text{Elo}_{\text{new, winner}} = \text{Elo}_{\text{old, winner}} + \Delta\text{Elo}\]
\[\text{Elo}_{\text{new, loser}} = \text{Elo}_{\text{old, loser}} - \Delta\text{Elo}\]

  filter(team %in% c("SEA", "NE")) %>%
  arrange(desc(elo)) %>%
  mutate(

    `Elo Rating` = round(elo, 1),
    `Win Probability` = paste0(round(sb_win_prob * 100, 1), "%")
  ) %>%
  select(Team, `Elo Rating`, `Win Probability`) %>%

The playoff period (shaded) shows both teams pulling away from the pack, but Seattle has a clear separation from the rest of the playoff contenders whereas New England has a similar Elo ranking.


2. Baseline Historical Model
The Elo approach is sophisticated but carries assumptions: teams have consistent “strength,” performance follows predictable patterns, and that a team will live up to historical performances. To provide a sanity check, I built a simpler baseline model to compare the Elo model to.
Method:

Collect all Super Bowl scores from 1967-2025 (59 games)
Extract scoring distributions for winners and losers
Adjust for each team’s 2025 season performance:

Points per game differential vs. league average
Strength of schedule adjustments
Home/road splits (though Super Bowl is neutral)

Simulate 10,000 possible games using Monte Carlo
Count outcomes

Why this approach? It’s transparent, requires minimal assumptions, and treats both teams “fairly” based purely on observable performance. If the Elo model and baseline model disagree wildly, something is probably wrong.

Historical Super Bowl Scoring Patterns
The baseline model uses scoring distributions from recent Super Bowls (2005-2025) to establish expected scoring patterns:


Show code
# Load Super Bowl history

# Focus on recent Super Bowls

  filter(season >= 2005, !is.na(away_score), !is.na(home_score)) %>%
  mutate(
    winner_score = pmax(away_score, home_score),
    loser_score = pmin(away_score, home_score)
  )

# Calculate statistics
sb_stats <- recent_sbs %>%
  summarise(
    `Games` = n(),
    `Winner Mean` = round(mean(winner_score), 1),
    `Winner SD` = round(sd(winner_score), 1),
    `Loser Mean` = round(mean(loser_score), 1),
    `Loser SD` = round(sd(loser_score), 1),
    `Total Mean` = round(mean(total_points), 1),
    `Total SD` = round(sd(total_points), 1)
  ) %>%
  mutate(
    Statistic = "Super Bowl Average (2005-2025)"
  ) %>%
  select(Statistic, `Games`, `Winner Mean`, `Winner SD`, `Loser Mean`, `Loser SD`, `Total Mean`, `Total SD`)

How Predicted Scores Are Calculated
The two models use different approaches to convert team ratings into expected final scores:
Elo Model Score Prediction:
The Elo model converts Elo rating differences into expected scores using historical Super Bowl patterns:
\[\text{Base Total} = \text{Mean total points from Super Bowls since 2010}\]
\[\text{Elo Impact} = (\text{SEA Elo} - \text{NE Elo}) \times 0.01\]
\[\text{SEA Expected Score} = \frac{\text{Base Total}}{2} + \text{Elo Impact}\]
\[\text{NE Expected Score} = \frac{\text{Base Total}}{2} - \text{Elo Impact}\]
Free Parameters: - 0.01: Elo-to-points conversion factor (1 Elo point ≈ 0.01 game points). This could be tuned by regressing historical Elo differences against actual score differences. - season >= 2010: Which Super Bowls to include in baseline. More recent games may better reflect modern scoring patterns. - Score bounds: max(10, min(40, score)) - reasonable limits to prevent unrealistic predictions.
Baseline Model Score Prediction:
The baseline model uses team performance relative to league average:
\[\text{Base Score} = \frac{\text{Mean Away Score} + \text{Mean Home Score}}{2} \text{ (from Super Bowls since 2005)}\]
\[\text{SEA Offense Adjustment} = \text{SEA Points For} - \text{League Average Points For}\]
\[\text{NE Defense Adjustment} = \text{League Average Points For} - \text{NE Points Against}\]
\[\text{SEA Expected Score} = \text{Base Score} + \text{SEA Offense Adjustment} - \text{NE Defense Adjustment}\]
\[\text{NE Expected Score} = \text{Base Score} + \text{NE Offense Adjustment} - \text{SEA Defense Adjustment}\]
The model then simulates 10,000 games using Poisson distributions with these expected scores as the mean (λ).
Free Parameters: - season >= 2005: Which Super Bowls to include in baseline. Could be adjusted to focus on more recent games. - Score bounds: max(10, min(45, score)) - reasonable limits for simulations. - n_sims = 10000: Number of simulations. More simulations = more stable results but slower computation.
Parameter Sensitivity Considerations:
These parameters could be tuned to improve predictions: - Elo conversion factor (0.01): Could be estimated from historical data by regressing Elo differences against actual score differences in Super Bowls. - Historical window: Using only recent Super Bowls (e.g., 2015+) might better reflect modern scoring patterns, but reduces sample size. - Score bounds: Current bounds are somewhat arbitrary. Could be based on historical extremes (lowest/highest Super Bowl scores). - Simulation count: 10,000 is a reasonable balance, but increasing to 100,000 would provide more stable percentiles at the cost of computation time.

Table 7 compares our model predictions to the betting market. The models align reasonably well with the betting market on total points (model average: 47 vs. market: 45.4166667), but the bookmakers show a more pronounced Seattle advantage. The betting market implies Seattle has approximately 69.6% win probability, while our models suggest 59.7%—a meaningful difference of about -9.9 percentage points. Both of our models agree on the same outcome as the betting markets, but the margin of that victory is different - there are a number of reasons why this discrepancy might exist, as dicussed in the following section.
Why the difference? Betting markets incorporate not just predictive power, but also betting patterns, public perception, and bookmaker risk management. Statistical models, by contrast, are purely about probability. The market may be accounting for factors like: - Public betting bias (favorite teams often get more action) - Sharp money vs. public money - Bookmaker risk management (lines move to balance action) - Intangible factors (coaching, playoff experience, “clutch” reputation)
Who’s right? The only way we can find out is after the game on Sunday. But it’s worth noting that both approaches have merit: the betting market reflects the collective wisdom of thousands of bettors and professional oddsmakers, while statistical models provide a data-driven baseline free from market psychology, individual bias and herd mentality. Bookmakers are famously good at calculating these odds - if they weren’t, they wouldn’t exist!

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
What The Models Can’t Know
Before declaring statistical supremacy, let’s be honest about the limitations. These predictions rely on season-long performance patterns, but they cannot account for:






WarningModel Blind Spots



In-game factors:

Key injuries (e.g., starting QB injured in 2nd quarter)
Coaching adjustments at halftime
Weather conditions (wind, rain, and/or snow affecting passing and running ability)
Referee decisions and controversial calls
Turnover luck and timing
Special teams breakdowns

Intangibles:

Individual “clutch” performances by star players
Momentum swings and psychological factors
Playoff experience and pressure
Motivation (“wanting it more”)
Pure randomness (fumble bounces, tipped interceptions)



These are not weaknesses to be embarrassed about — it’s an honest acknowledgment of what statistical models can and cannot do. Sports wouldn’t be worth watching if they were perfectly predictable.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
Interpreting Probabilistic Predictions
A 60% win probability is not a confident prediction for the Super Bowl outcome. Let me put this in perspective:
If we could somehow replay this exact Super Bowl matchup 100 times (same teams, same preparation, same conditions), Seattle would win about 60 times and New England about 40 times. That means:

2 out of every 5 times, New England wins. This is far from impossible.
If New England wins on Sunday, it doesn’t mean the model was “wrong”—it means we observed one of the 40% outcomes.
Conversely, if Seattle wins, it doesn’t definitively validate the model.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
Why This Prediction Is Interesting
You might wonder: why bother with statistical models when bookmakers already have Seattle as a significant favorite? The betting market shows Seattle -4.5 with approximately 70% win probability—why do we need models that suggest a more modest 60% advantage?
Here’s what makes this analysis valuable:

1. Going against the bookies’
The betting market reflects not just predictive power, but also public sentiment, betting patterns, and bookmaker risk management. When thousands of bettors pile onto the favorite, lines can move beyond pure probability, in order for bookmakers to cover themselves in the event of the favourites winning. Our statistical models, by contrast, are purely data-driven — they don’t care about narratives, “gut feelings,” or herd mentality. The fact that both approaches agree on the outcome (Seattle wins) but differ on the margin is itself informative. It suggests the market may be incorporating factors beyond statistical probability—whether those factors are valuable insights or market inefficiencies, Sunday will reveal.


2. Quantifying uncertainty honestly
The bookmakers’ 70% win probability suggests a confident prediction. Our models’ 60% suggests more caution. Rather than declaring “Seattle will dominate,” we’re saying “Seattle has a meaningful but not overwhelming advantage.” This is more honest about the inherent randomness in a single game. If Seattle wins by 16 points, the bookmakers were right about the margin. If it’s a close game, the models’ caution may prove more accurate. Either way, we learn something.


3. Testing statistical methods
By locking in predictions before the game, this becomes a controlled experiment. If the bookmakers’ more emphatic prediction proves correct, it suggests factors like:

Playoff experience and “clutch” performance
Coaching matchups and game-planning
Intangible team chemistry and momentum
Public betting patterns that reflect insider knowledge

If the models’ more cautious prediction proves closer, it suggests that statistical fundamentals (Elo ratings, season performance) are sufficient, and market psychology may be overconfident. Either outcome provides valuable data for improving future models.


4. Appreciating unpredictability
The 10 percentage point difference between market (70%) and models (60%) isn’t a bug—it’s a feature. If the models are wrong, we’ll have concrete evidence of what variables to include in future iterations. Perhaps we need to:

Weight recent playoff performance more heavily
Account for individual performances and coaching experience
Incorporate factors the market sees but our models can’t capture

This is how statistical models improve: by making predictions, testing them, and learning from the gaps.

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
What Happens if I’m wrong?
Learning from Every Outcome:

If Seattle wins by 1-7 points: Models were well-calibrated
If Seattle wins by 10+: Models underestimated their dominance
If New England wins close: This was in the 40% probability window
If New England dominates: Models missed something fundamental about playoff football

title: Predicting the Unpredictable: A Statistical Exploration of Super Bowl LX
text:
Conclusion: The Honest Statistician’s Role
NFL teams, sports broadcasters and bookmakers have access to proprietary data, advanced metrics, and decades of institutional knowledge. Yet games remain stubbornly unpredictable. This is a good thing.
If sports were perfectly predictable, there would be no point in watching them. The reason we tune in isn’t to see the inevitable unfold — it’s to witness the uncertainty, the improbable, and occasional shock results. This is what makes sport exciting.
The statistician’s role isn’t to spoil the magic by eliminating uncertainty, it’s to:

Quantify uncertainty honestly (60-40, not 100-0)
Test models rigorously (with pre-game predictions)
Learn from outcomes (what did we miss?)
Appreciate randomness (that’s what makes sports entertaining)

So here’s my final prediction, locked in before kickoff:

text:
Technical Appendix
For those interested in implementation details:

Data Sources
All data from nflverse: - nflreadr::load_schedules() for game results (2015-2025) - nflfastR::load_pbp() for play-by-play data (2025 season) - Full reproducible code on GitHub
Elo Model Inspiration:
This Elo implementation is inspired by FiveThirtyEight’s NFL Elo model, which used similar principles of rating teams based on game outcomes and margin of victory. Sadly, this website and its Elo model have been taken down and are now owned by ABC news - this is why the website is archived and will be redirected to ABC’s home page. While our implementation uses slightly different parameters (K-factor, home advantage, regression), the core methodology follows the same Elo rating system that has been successfully applied to NFL predictions for over a decade.


Model Specifications
Elo Implementation:


Show code
# Elo update function
update_elo <- function(winner_elo, loser_elo, margin, k = 20, home_advantage = 65) {
  # Expected win probability
  expected_win <- 1 / (1 + 10^((loser_elo - winner_elo - home_advantage)/400))
  
  # Margin of victory multiplier
  mov_multiplier <- log(abs(margin) + 1)
  
  # Calculate Elo change
  elo_change <- k * mov_multiplier * (1 - expected_win)
  
  winner_new <- winner_elo + elo_change
  loser_new <- loser_elo - elo_change
  
  return(list(winner = winner_new, loser = loser_new))
}


Score Prediction Equations:
Both models predict final scores using different approaches:
1. Elo Model Score Prediction:
The Elo model converts Elo ratings into expected scores using historical Super Bowl scoring patterns:
\[\text{Base Total} = \text{Mean total points from Super Bowls since 2010}\]
\[\text{Elo Impact} = (\text{SEA Elo} - \text{NE Elo}) \times 0.01\]
\[\text{SEA Expected Score} = \frac{\text{Base Total}}{2} + \text{Elo Impact}\]
\[\text{NE Expected Score} = \frac{\text{Base Total}}{2} - \text{Elo Impact}\]
Free Parameters: - 0.01: Elo-to-points conversion factor (1 Elo point ≈ 0.01 game points). This could be tuned based on historical data. - season >= 2010: Which Super Bowls to include in baseline calculation. More recent games may be more relevant. - Score bounds: max(10, min(40, score)) - reasonable limits to prevent unrealistic predictions.
2. Baseline Model Score Prediction:
The baseline model uses team performance relative to league average:
\[\text{Base Score} = \frac{\text{Mean Away Score} + \text{Mean Home Score}}{2} \text{ (from Super Bowls since 2005)}\]
\[\text{SEA Offense Adjustment} = \text{SEA Points For} - \text{League Average Points For}\]
\[\text{NE Defense Adjustment} = \text{League Average Points For} - \text{NE Points Against}\]
\[\text{SEA Expected Score} = \text{Base Score} + \text{SEA Offense Adjustment} - \text{NE Defense Adjustment}\]
\[\text{NE Expected Score} = \text{Base Score} + \text{NE Offense Adjustment} - \text{SEA Defense Adjustment}\]
The model then simulates 10,000 games using Poisson distributions with these expected scores as the mean (λ).
Free Parameters: - season >= 2005: Which Super Bowls to include in baseline. Could be adjusted to focus on more recent games. - Score bounds: max(10, min(45, score)) - reasonable limits for simulations. - n_sims = 10000: Number of simulations. More simulations = more stable results but slower computation.
Parameter Sensitivity:
These parameters could be tuned to improve predictions:

Elo conversion factor (0.01): Could be estimated from historical data by regressing Elo differences against actual score differences.
Historical window: Using only recent Super Bowls (e.g., 2015+) might better reflect modern scoring patterns.
Score bounds: Current bounds (10-40 for Elo, 10-45 for Baseline) are somewhat arbitrary and could be based on historical extremes.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
text:
Football is the most popular sport in the World. With an estimated 5 billion fans worldwide according to n.d. (n.d.), it is unique in its ability to generate a feeling of community amongst fans. It also presents participants and observers with opportunities to make considerable sums of money. As such, the generation of accurate football prediction models has become a topic of intense interest among statisticians and data scientists.
In this article we will describe an approach to football modelling structured around an object called a vine copula. It can be read as a tutorial on statistical methodology, for which football provides motivation and context, or as a serious suggestion for sports analysts and enthusiasts looking for new ways to reconcile the many forms of data collected from football matches.
We will begin by introducing copulas: starting with relatively simple bivariate copulas, then moving on to more complicated vine copulas. Along the way we will demonstrate how they can be fitted to real data with the help of the python package vinecopulib. By the end of the post we will be in a position to generate probabilistic predictions from a vine copula, which could inform the decisions of sports analysts and bettors.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
text:
Bivariate copulas
While copula functions can theoretically be used to describe any number of random variables, they are most commonly used to model variables two at a time. A bivariate copula function \(C: [0,1]^2 \mapsto [0,1]\) is used to assign joint probabilities to events in which a pair of marginally uniform random variables \((U,V)\) fall in particular regions of the unit square. Specifically, we write \[\begin{align}
C(u,v) = P(U \leq u, V \leq v), && u,v \in [0,1],
\end{align}\] and insist that \[\begin{align}
C(u,0) = C(0,v) = 0, && C(u,1) =P(U\leq u)= u, && C(1,v) =P(V\leq v)= v,
\end{align}\] in order to satisfy the assumption of uniform marginals. It is also necessary for \(C\) to satisfy a `non-decreasing’ property ensuring that all rectangular subregions of \([0,1]^2\) are assigned non-negative probability.
Copulas are useful primarily because we can use them to describe the dependence between random variables via their dependence after having been passed through their own cumulative density functions, a transformation that renders them marginally uniformly distributed. Accordingly, we can write \[\begin{align}
P(X \leq x,Y \leq y)
&= P(F_X(X) \leq F_X(x), F_Y(Y) \leq F_Y(y)) \notag\\
&= P(U \leq u, V \leq v) \notag\\
&= C(u,v),
\end{align}\] where \(u=F_X(x)\) and \(v=F_Y(y)\) are the cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) for our random variables evaluated at \(x\) and \(y\), respectively. A central result in the copula literature, known as Sklar’s Theorem and published in Sklar (1959), formalizes the idea that for every function \(P(X \leq x,Y \leq y)\) there exists a corresponding \(C\) and that when \(X,Y\) are continous rabdom variables \(C\) is unique.
For pairs of continuous random variables we can write their joint probability density function as the mixed derivative of their joint cumulative distribution function \[
f(x,y) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}\frac{\partial}{\partial y} P(X \leq x,Y \leq y) = \frac{\partial u}{\partial x}\frac{\partial v}{\partial y} \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\frac{\partial}{\partial v}  C(u,v) = f_X(x) f_Y(y) c(u,v)
\tag{1}\] where \[\begin{align}
\frac{\partial u}{\partial x} = f_X(x), && \frac{\partial v}{\partial y} = f_Y(y), && \frac{\partial}{\partial u}\frac{\partial}{\partial v}  C(u,v) = c(u,v)
\end{align}\] from which we see how the copula allows us to factorize a joint density into a pair of marginal densities, \(f_X(x)\) and \(f_Y(y)\), and a copula density function \(c(u,v)\). In doing so we decompose the problem of specifying a joint distribution into more manageable sub-problems.
Upon rearranging, Equation 1 also implies that \[
f(x \mid y) = \frac{f(x,y)}{f_Y(y)} = f_X(x) \, c(u,v),
\tag{2}\] which is a result we will use in the sections to come. Specifically, it will allow us to switch out conditional densities with products of marginal densities and copula densities when we have more than two random variables to deal with.

Bivariate copula examples

Gaussian bivariate copula
\[\begin{equation}
C_{\text{Gauss}}(u,v;\rho) = \Phi_\rho (\Phi^{-1}(u), \Phi^{-1}(v)), \quad \rho \in (-1,1).
\end{equation}\] where \(\Phi\) is the CDF for a unit Normal random variable and \(\Phi_\rho\) is the joint CDF for a pair of bivariate Normal random variables with mean zero and correlation coefficient \(\rho\).


Frank’s bivariate copula
\[\begin{equation}
C_{\text{Frank}}(u,v) = -\kappa_F^{-1} \log \left\{ 1-\frac{ (1-\exp (-\kappa_F u)) (1-\exp(-\kappa_F v)) }{ 1-\exp(-\kappa_F) } \right\}, \quad \kappa_F \in [-∞,∞]\backslash \{0\}.
\end{equation}\]


Clayton’s bivariate copula
\[\begin{equation}
C_{\text{Clayton}}(u,v) = \max\left\{(u^{-\kappa_C}+v^{-\kappa_C}-1)^{-1/\kappa_C},0\right\},\quad \quad \kappa_C \in (0,∞].
\end{equation}\] The parameters \(\rho\), \(\kappa_F\) and \(\kappa_C\) are parameters that we can adjust to better match the relevant copula functions to observed distributions of data.


Independence copula
\[\begin{equation}
C_{\text{Ind}}(u,v) = uv.
\end{equation}\] The independence copula, with no parameters, is arguably trivial but is often selected on the basis of its AIC when the number of observations available for fitting is small.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
section: Selecting bivariate copulas for their tail behviour
text:
Selecting bivariate copulas for their tail behviour
Selection of the parameter values that determine the shape of a particular copula function is typically performed via gradient-based optimization of the log-likelihood. Selection between distinct families of copula function (like the Gaussian, Frank and Clayton families) tends to be done on the basis of their AIC or BIC. In practice, the copula function that fits best to a given data set is often determined by the functions’ behaviour in the corners of the unit square.
This behaviour is characterized by Czado (2019) using quantities referred to as lower- and upper-tail dependence coefficients. They are defined as \[\begin{align}
\lambda_{lower} &= \lim_{t\to 0^+} P(Y \leq F_Y^{-1}(t) \mid X \leq F_X^{-1}(t))=\lim_{t\to 0^+}\frac{C(t,t)}{t},\\
\lambda_{upper} &= \lim_{t\to 1^-} P(Y > F_Y^{-1}(t)\mid X> F_X^{-1}(t))=\lim_{t\to 1^-}\frac{1-2t+C(t,t)}{1-t}.
\end{align}\] These quantities answer questions of the form: ‘if \(X\) is observed to be far into the tail of its marginal distribution, how probable is it that \(Y\) is just as far into the tail of its marginal?’. They are describing the cooccurrence of extreme values. In the context of the football data we might imagine, for example, that the home team receiving an anomolously large number of yellow cards might increase the probability of the away team receiving just as many yellow cards because the match has become exceedingly aggressive and disorderly. We might also imagine a large number of home yellows being due to match-specific discipline problems that the away team can mostly rise above so that the number of away yellows is not correspondingly high. The choice between these two hypotheses regarding team behaviours maps approximately onto the choice between copulas with different degrees of (upper) tail dependence.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
section: Bivariate copulas for discrete random variables
text:
Bivariate copulas for discrete random variables
Unlike a continuous random variable, a discrete random variable cannot be transformed in such a way that it has a (continuous) uniform distribution. So it might look like the copula definition above is useless to us in the discrete setting. Perhaps the main problem, as Genest and Nešlehová (2007) and Geenens (2020) explain in detail, is that the one-to-one correspondence between bivariate cumulative mass functions and copula functions is lost.
However, given the obvious importance of discrete count data in football, we will persevere! Copula densities, whose logarithm we maximize when fitting to observations of continuous random variables, are avoided in the dicrete setting. Instead, for discrete \(X_1, X_2\) we evaluate probabilities, which are subsequently logged and maximized with respect to a copula parameter \(\kappa\). These probabilities can be identified with integrals over rectangles of densities (such as those in Figure 1). An inclusion-exclusion technique is used to derive the integral over a rectangle in the interior of \([0,1]^2\) in terms of rectangles, each of which have a corner at \((0,0)\). Explicitly, we write \[\begin{equation}
P(X_1 = x_1, X_2 = x_2) = C(u_1, u_2; \kappa) - C(u_1^-, u_2; \kappa) - C(u_1, u_2^-; \kappa) + C(u_1^-, u_2^-; \kappa)
\end{equation}\] where \(u_1^-\) and \(u_2^-\) are the left-sided limits of the CDFs of \(X_1\) and \(X_2\) at \(x_1\) and \(x_2\), respectively.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
section: The pair copula constructions in three dimensions
text:
The pair copula constructions in three dimensions
A three dimensional probability density function can be decomposed into a product of conditional densities, \[\begin{align}
f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = f(x_1) f(x_2 \mid x_1) f(x_3 \mid x_2,x_1).
\end{align}\] For convenience we can define conditional random variables \(x_{3 \mid 1} = x_3 \mid x_1\) and \(x_{2 \mid 1} = x_2 \mid x_1\) and write \[\begin{align}
f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = f(x_1) f(x_2 \mid x_1) f(x_{3 \mid 1} \mid x_{2\mid 1}).
\end{align}\] We can now switch out the conditional densities for products of marginal and copula densities according to Equation 2, i.e. \[\begin{align}
f(x_2 \mid x_1) = f(x_2) c_{12}(u_1,u_2), && f(x_{3 \mid 1} \mid x_{2 \mid 1}) = f(x_{3\mid 1}) c_{23 \mid 1}(u_{2 \mid 1},u_{3 \mid 1}).
\end{align}\] We can use our switching trick again to get rid of the \(f(x_{3\mid 1})\) above \[\begin{align}
f(x_{3\mid 1}) = f(x_{3} \mid x_{1}) = f(x_3) c_{13}(u_1,u_3).
\end{align}\] Substituting these terms back in and collect terms, we get \[
f(x_1,x_2,x_3) = f(x_1)f(x_2)f(x_3) \, c_{12}(u_1,u_2) c_{13}(u_1,u_3) c_{23 \mid 1}(u_{2 \mid 1},u_{3 \mid 1}),
\tag{3}\] a product of marginal densities and bivariate copula densities.
At this point we make an important assumption - one that we will need in order for downsteam calculations to be tractable. We will need to assume that the bivariate copula density functions involving conditioned variables (e.g. the function \(c_{23 \mid 1}\) above) do not depend on the value of the random variable conditioned on. This is referred to as the ‘simplifying assumption’ in the copula literature.
If you are extemely alert and careful, you may have noticed that, like a magician, I have slipped a couple of things past you. Firstly, I decomposed the joint densities as a product of conditional densities that seems natural if we imagine the variables \(x_1\), \(x_2\) and \(x_3\) being produced in that order, but I needn’t have. Any ordering would have done. Secondly, I arbitrarily decided to define some new variables conditioned on \(x_1\). However, at that point, I could have defined \(x_{3 \mid 2} = x_3 \mid x_2\) and \(x_{1 \mid 2} = x_1 \mid x_2\) and continued the rest of the operations to arrive at an expression that looks slightly different from the one we actually produced (one with the subscripts \(1\) and \(2\) swapped around).
The point is that the PCC is not unique. The choices we make along the way involving the ordering of the variables change the expression we end up with and the simplfying assumption means that, in general, the different expressions we end up with really are different - they are not, in general, the same expressions in disguise.
Before moving on to the next section it will be useful to set up some extra notation and to define an object known as an \(h\)-function. It is nothing more the distribution function for a random variable conditional on another taking a particular value. For example, for random variables \(X_1\), \(X_2\), \(U_1=F_{X_1}(X_1)\), \(U_2=F_{X_2}(X_2)\) we would write the \(h\)-function \[\begin{align}
h(u_1|u_2) &:= \frac{\partial}{\partial u_2} C(u_1,u_2) \\
&= P(U_1 \leq u_1, U_2=u_2)\\
&= P(U_1 \leq u_1 \mid U_2=u_2)P(U_2=u_2)\\
&= P(U_1 \leq u_1 \mid U_2=u_2)\\
&= P(X_1 \leq x_1 \mid X_2=x_2)
\end{align}\] where, strictly speaking, the quantity \(P(U_2=u_2)\) is a uniform probability density (equal to one for all values) rather than a probability.
Vine copulas are useful for thinking about and keeping track of very large numbers of possible pair copula constructions. This is particularly important in high dimensions where the number of possible decompositions increases very quickly. Morales-Nápoles et al. (2023) showed that the number of regular vines on \(d\) variables is \[\begin{align}
\frac{1}{2} \ d! \ 2^{\binom{d-2}{2}},
\end{align}\] meaning that in four dimensions there are 24 decompositions, in six dimensions there are 23040 and in eight dimensions there are 660602880.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
text:
PCCs as sequences of trees
The key conceptual breakthrough that provided statisticians with a way to stitch together bivariate copulas in a systematic way appears to have been made independently by H. Joe and R.M. Cooke. The breakthrough was to identify the bivariate copula densities in products such as Equation 3 with edges in trees. More precisely, they proposed using a set of trees that gradually reduce in size. In the example above with three variables there are two copula densities, \(c_{12}\) and \(c_{13}\), that do not involve conditioned variables and one copula density, \(c_{23 \mid 1}\), that does. The first two copula densities are represented as edges in the first tree, which has three nodes corresponding to the three variables. The second tree has two nodes corresponding to the two edges in the first tree and one edge corresponding to the copula density involving conditioned variables.
A vine copula on \(d\) dimensions is a sequence of \(d-1\) trees, each of which has a particular structure that ensures the necessary building blocks are in place for the next tree in the sequence. The first tree has \(d\) nodes corresponding to the \(d\) variables and \(d-1\) edges corresponding to the \(d-1\) bivariate copula densities that do not involve conditioned variables. The second tree has \(d-1\) nodes corresponding to the \(d-1\) edges in the first tree and \(d-2\) edges corresponding to the \(d-2\) bivariate copula densities involving one conditioned variable. The third tree has \(d-2\) nodes corresponding to the \(d-2\) edges in the second tree and \(d-3\) edges corresponding to the \(d-3\) bivariate copula densities involving two conditioned variables. This process continues until we have a final tree with two nodes and one edge corresponding to the single bivariate copula density involving \(d-2\) conditioned variables.
Czado (2019) describes the vine construction more formally as a set of trees \(\mathbb{V}=\{T_1,...,T_{d-1}\}\) satisfying the following conditions:
\[\begin{array}{l}
\text{(1) Each tree } T_{j}=\left(N_{j}, E_{j}\right) \text{ is connected, i.e. for all nodes } a, b \in T_{j}, j=1, \ldots, d-1 \text{,}\\
\quad \text{ there exists a path } n_{1}, \ldots, n_{k} \subset N_{j} \text{ with } a=n_{1}, b=n_{k} \text{.}\\
\text{(2) } T_{1} \text{ is a tree with node set } N_{1}=\{1, \ldots, d\} \text{ and edge set } E_{1} \text{.}\\
\text{(3) For } j \geq 2, T_{j} \text{ is a tree with node set } N_{j}=E_{j-1} \text{ and edge set } E_{j} \text{.}\\
\text{(4) [Proximity Condition] For } j=2, \ldots, d-1 \text{ and } \{a, b\} \in E_{j} \text{ it must hold that } |a \cap b|=1 \text{.}\end{array}\]
\((1)\) ensures at each tree level all nodes are connected, \((2)\) ensures that nodes in the first tree denote the \(d\) variables, \((3)\) ensures that for all trees after the first the edge set of the previous tree become our new nodes and finally \((4)\) ensures that for any two nodes to be connected in trees after the first, the corresponding edges in the previous tree must share a common node. This ‘proximity condition’ ensures the building blocks required for the higher level conditioning exist in the decomposition.

title: Modelling Football Data with Vine Copulas
section: A vine copula for football data
text:
A vine copula for football data
In this example we will look at some real football data collected over 5 years of Premier League matches. The full data, which at the time of writing can be accessed at https://www.football-data.co.uk/, contains tens of variables relating mostly to event counts of different types and bookmakers’ odds. For our current purposes it will be convenient to pick a subset of six count variables: home goals (\(HG\)), away goals (\(AG\)), home shots (\(HS\)), away shots (\(AS\)), home yellow cards (\(HY\)) and away yellow cards (\(AY\)).
While there are over 20 thousand of possible vine structures in six dimensions, not all will fit the data equally well. As explained in greater depth in Dissmann et al. (2013), the most common approach to selecting a particular vine structure is to use a maximum spanning Tree algorithm (MST). Typically, the MST algorithm is provided with the absolute value of Kendall’s tau (or some other correlation metric such as Spearman’s rho) between all pairs of variables. It then finds the tree that connects all variables in such a way that the sum of correlations between connected variables is maximized.
Once the MST has chosen the tree structure, bivariate copulas are fitted via maximum likelihood to each pair of variables for which the tree has an edge. As mentioned above, we can also select between copula families using AIC-type criteria.



Figure 2. A fully connected graph between the six football variables showing absolute value kendalls tau between paired variables, with a path in red showing the maximum spanning tree



Choosing the vine’s trees

Tree 1
The edges marked in red in Figure 2 represent the maximum spanning tree for the fully-connected graph of football variables. This tree will be used as the first tree in our vine.
For clarity we redraw the tree below. At the same time we modify our notation slightly, switching the variable names for numbers (\(HS=1\), \(AS=2\), \(HY=3\), \(AY=4\), \(HG=5\), \(AG=6\)), to better match the expressions in the previous sections. We will also label the tree’s edges with tuples identifying the nodes that they connect. These are the tuples that appear in the subscripts of the copula densities that will, eventually, contribute to the final vine copula density.



Figure 3. The first tree in the vine with variable names replaced with corresponding numbers, specfically the pairs (3,4),(1,3),(1,2),(1,5) and (2,6) have been selected.


In our example we fit bivariate copulas between the pairs of variables \((1,2)\), \((1,3)\), \((1,5)\), \((2,6)\) and \((3,4)\). Their corresponding copula densities (\(c_{12}, c_{13}, c_{15}, c_{26}, c_{34}\)) will be carried all the way through the vine-building algorithm, contributing as factors to our final expression for the full copula density.
Note that by maximizing the sum of correlations at this stage, without full consideration of how we are setting ourselves up for the next tree in the sequence, we are not necessarily maximizing the overall likelihood of the vine. The approach is one of greedy optimization, which is not guaranteed to find a globally optimal vine, but has been shown to be relatively successful in practice.


Tree 2
The edges from Tree 1 now become nodes to be paired up by Tree 2. In this ‘meta-tree’ setting our rule for identifying new edges becomes slightly more complicated. Firstly, edges can now only form between nodes that share a common variable in the previous tree. For example, the nodes \((1,3)\) and \((3,4)\) can be connected by an edge in Tree 2 because they both share variable \(3\) in Tree 1. However, the nodes \((1,3)\) and \((2,6)\) cannot be connected by an edge in Tree 2 because they share no common variable in Tree 1. This is Czado’s proximity condition. The three trees obeying the proximity condition are presented in Figure 4, where each colour represents a valid tree.



Figure 4. A graph showing all possible second trees in the vine satisfying to the proximity condition, each shown using a different colour.


The second issue to address is how we are to interpret the edges in Tree 2. Each edge corresponds to a bivariate copula density involving one conditioned variable. For example, the edge connecting nodes \((1,3)\) and \((3,4)\) corresponds to the bivariate copula density \(c_{1,4;3}\), which is the density of the copula relating \(X_1\) and \(X_4\) conditional on \(X_3\). More generally, edges correspond to bivariate copulas for the set differences of the tuple of numbers in the nodes they connect. They are conditioned on the intersection of the tuple of numbers in the nodes they connect.
The bivariate copulas themselves are fitted to pseudo-observations, which are generated by applying the h-function for the relevant copulas to the original observations. For example, for the edge connecting nodes \((1,3)\) and \((3,4)\) in Tree 2 we define the pseudo-observations derived from the copula functions fitted in Tree 1 \[\begin{align}
u_{1|3}= h_{1|3}(u_1|u_3) = \frac{\partial}{\partial u_3} C_{1,3}(u_1,u_3)\\
u_{4|3}= h_{4|3}(u_4|u_3) = \frac{\partial}{\partial u_3} C_{1,4}(u_4,u_3).
\end{align}\] The choice of nodes to join with edges, and the corresponding bivariate copulas to fit, is determined by the MST algorithm again. This time the MST is provided with the absolute value of Kendall’s tau between the pseudo-observations.
Suppose according to the MST the optimal tree chosen is the tree represented in pink. We can then add the corresponding edge labels:



Figure 5. The selected, according to maximum spanning tree, second tree in the vine. Now we have the edges (1,4 given 3),(3,5 given 1),(2,3 given 1),(1,6 given 2).


The edge labels are the same as the subscripts on the corresponding copula functions.


Tree 3
Construction Tree 3 involves repeating the process used for Tree 2. We look for edges that satisfy the proximity condition, transform variables using h-functions to produce pseudo-observations, use the MST to select a tree, and choose bivariate copula families and estimate their associated parameters via maximum likelihood.
Tree 3 for our football data looks like this:



Figure 6. Third tree in the vine, now have the edges (2,4 given 1,3),(2,5 given 1,3) and (3,6 given 1,2).




Tree 4
Tree 4 looks like this:



Figure 7. Fourth tree in the vine, with the edges (4,6 given 1,2,3) and (5,6 given 1,2,3).




Tree 5
And Tree 5 looks like this:



Figure 8. Fifth and final tree in the vine, with the single edge (4,5 given 1,2,3,6).




Piecing it all together
The final copula density can then be found by multiplying all of the bivariate copulas from each of the trees. In this example we have: \[\begin{align}
c(u_1,u_2,u_3,u_4,u_5,u_6) = &\underbrace{c_{45;1,2,3,6}(C_{4|1,2,3,6},C_{4|1,2,3,6})}_{\text{tree 5}} \\
&\underbrace{c_{56;1,2,3}(C_{5|1,2,3},C_{6|1,2,3})\cdot c_{46;1,2,3}(C_{4|1,2,3},C_{6|1,2,3})}_{\text{tree 4}} \\
&\underbrace{c_{36;1,2}(C_{3|1,2},C_{6|1,2})\cdot c_{25;1,3}(C_{2|1,3},C_{5|1,3})\cdot c_{24;1,3}(C_{2|1,3},C_{4|1,3})}_{\text{tree 3}} \\
&\underbrace{c_{16;2}(C_{1|2},C_{6|2})\cdot c_{23:1}(C_{2|1},C_{3|1}) \cdot c_{35;1}(C_{3|1},C_{5|1})\cdot c_{1,4;3}(C_{1|3},C_{4|3})}_{\text{tree 2}} \\
&\underbrace{c_{26}\cdot c_{12} \cdot c_{15} \cdot c_{13} \cdot c_{34}}_{\text{tree 1}}
\end{align}\] where we have omitted \(u_i\)’s and parameters to simplify notation.

Fitting a vine copula to the football data
We start by installing and loading the packages we’ll need % pip install pyvinecopulib % pip install scikit-learn


Code
import pyvinecopulib as pv
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split;
from IPython.display import display, Markdown
from scipy.stats import nbinom, poisson, lognorm


We then transform the count data with the cumulative mass functions of marginal distributions we have chosen for them. In this case these are a mixture of negative binomial and Poisson distributions whose parameters are chosen to match the first moments of the data. We also transform the counts one less than the observed ones in order to compute the left-sided limits of the discontinuous CDFs. This is acheived using the \(\verb|loc|\) argument for the CDF functions.


Code
seasons = ['2122', '2223', '2324', '2425', '2526']
columns_to_keep = ['FTHG', 'FTAG', 'HY', 'AY', 'HS', 'AS', 'B365H', 'B365D', 'B365A']
dfs = [pd.read_csv(f'E0_{season}.csv')[columns_to_keep].copy() for season in seasons]
X = pd.concat(dfs, axis=0, join='inner', ignore_index=True)

q1 = np.mean(X['HS'])/np.var(X['HS'])
n1 = np.mean(X['HS'])**2/(np.var(X['HS'])-np.mean(X['HS']))
u1 = nbinom.cdf(X['HS'], n1, q1)
um1 = nbinom.cdf(X['HS'], n1, q1,loc=1)

q2 = np.mean(X['AS'])/np.var(X['AS'])
n2 = np.mean(X['AS'])**2/(np.var(X['AS'])-np.mean(X['AS']))
u2 = nbinom.cdf(X['AS'], n2, q2)          
um2 = nbinom.cdf(X['AS'], n2, q2,loc=1)

u3 = poisson.cdf(X['HY'], np.mean(X['HY']))
um3 = poisson.cdf(X['HY'], np.mean(X['HY']), loc=1)

u4 = poisson.cdf(X['AY'], np.mean(X['AY']))
um4 = poisson.cdf(X['AY'], np.mean(X['AY']), loc=1)

u5 = poisson.cdf(X['FTHG'], np.mean(X['FTHG']))
um5 = poisson.cdf(X['FTHG'], np.mean(X['FTHG']), loc=1)

u6 = poisson.cdf(X['FTAG'], np.mean(X['FTAG']))
um6 = poisson.cdf(X['FTAG'], np.mean(X['FTAG']), loc=1)

uniform_data = np.column_stack((u1,u2,u3,u4,u5,u6,um1,um2,um3,um4,um5,um6))
uni_train, uni_test = train_test_split(uniform_data, test_size=0.2, random_state=42)


Once we have the uniform margins we can move onto fitting the vine. At this point the vinecopulib package provides with many options. We can choose, for example:

which bivariate copula families to try out on selected pairs of variables,
the selection criteria used to choose a family,
whether to truncate the vine (that is to set all bivariate copulas to the independence copula, \(C(u,v) = uv\)) after a given tree depth).

This can be done as follows:

chosen_candidate_families = [

    pv.BicopFamily.clayton,
    pv.BicopFamily.frank,

chosen_controls = pv.FitControlsVinecop(
    family_set=chosen_candidate_families,
    allow_rotations=True,
    selection_criterion='aic'
)


A full list of controls can be found in the pyvinecopulib documentation.
We can now let the package loose on the data. It will do all the hard work we have described - looking for trees maximizing sums of pairwise absolute correlations and trying out different bivariate copulas on the edges.

RVine =  pv.Vinecop.from_data(uni_train, var_types=["d"] * 6, controls=chosen_controls)

section: Simulating football data with a vine copula
text:
Simulating football data with a vine copula
When predicting the events of a football match it would be disadvantageous to ignore bookmakers odds. We will want to condition on them somehow in our simulations, and there are multiple strategies for doing so.
One strategy involves fitting a vine jointly to the odds data and the count data, but in a way that strictly preserves an ordering of the variables. Those that are to be conditioned on need to appear at the beginning so that we can substitute in observed values during the simulation process. Typically, the ordering is enforced by insisting that the vine’s first tree is a path graph (or linear graph). This constraint filters through to the other trees via the proximity condition.
An alternative strategy is to pre-condition all our count data on the bookmakers odds. One way to do this is to fit Poisson GLMs to our count data. For each match and each count variable the GLM’s predictive distribution can be used as the marginal. From this point onwards the vine fitting procedure described in the preceding sections an be applied.
In the code chunk below we fit Poisson GLMs


Code
from sklearn.linear_model import PoissonRegressor

X['log_odds_ratio'] = np.log(X['B365A'] / X['B365H'])
X_predictor = X[['log_odds_ratio']]
ignore_cols = ['B365H', 'B365A', 'log_odds_ratio']
target_cols = [col for col in X.columns if col not in ignore_cols]
fitted_models = {}

for target in target_cols:
    y = X[target]
    model = PoissonRegressor(alpha=0, max_iter=1000)
    model.fit(X_predictor, y)
    fitted_values = model.predict(X_predictor)
    fitted_models[target] = {
        'model': model,
        'intercept': model.intercept_,
        'coefficient': model.coef_[0],
        'fitted_values': fitted_values
    }


before computing the \(u\) values as before


Code
stats = ['HS', 'AS', 'HY', 'AY', 'FTHG', 'FTAG']
u_list = []
um_list = []

for stat in stats:
    mu = fitted_models[stat]['fitted_values']
    u_list.append(poisson.cdf(X[stat], mu))
    um_list.append(poisson.cdf(X[stat], mu, loc=1))

uniform_data = np.column_stack(u_list + um_list)
RVine = pv.Vinecop.from_data(uniform_data, var_types=["d"] * 6, controls=chosen_controls)


We now pass the simulated \(u\) values through the inverse CDFs conditional on the bookmakers’ odds for a match we want to predict (below we use log odds of zero, corresponding to equal implied winning probabilities for the two teams).


Code
n_sims = 9999
u_sim = RVine.simulate(n=n_sims)
X_sim = {}
for i, stat in enumerate(stats):
    mu = np.exp(fitted_models[stat]['intercept'] + fitted_models[stat]['coefficient'] * 0)
    u_col = u_sim[:, i]
    X_sim[stat] = poisson.ppf(u_col, mu)
X_sim_df = pd.DataFrame(X_sim)

title: How Efficient is Basketball?
text:
Basketball is one of the youngest widely played team sports in the world. Over its short history it has grown from its roots in the YMCA to global popularity, with even derivative forms being played as Olympic competition. There have been several developments that have reformed the game, such as the introduction of the shot clock, the three point line and liberalisation of the rules regarding dunking. A feature practically unique to basketball however is the common occurrence of high-scoring, but still close, games. In a game both teams often score more than 100 points each while the final winning margin will be less than 3 points, meaning that the outcome could have been reversed by one more scoring event. Between the 2016-17 and the 2024-25 season, both teams scored more than 100 in 65% of the 10,740 games played. 18% of these high-scoring games finished within 3 points. Last-gasp winners exist in many sports, but not many of these last-gasp winners are only the last of (on average) 116 equivalent events.
While similar scoring dynamics are present in games like tennis or badminton, in those sports the aim is to reach a certain point total, rather than scoring the most points within a given time period. Rugby matches can have the similar turnarounds, but the number of scoring events is much lower. Time-limited close games certainly lead to exciting contests.

This dynamic does suggest that the game is sometimes won by whichever team scores last. Given the rapid turnovers of possessions in a basketball game, could the outcome be a 50/50 coin toss? Obviously this is an oversimplification, as some teams can win games consistently, with the Golden State Warriors & the Boston Celtics both consistently producing high winning percentages in recent years. In close games, the final seconds of game time can often be extended by breaks in play such as timeouts and the efficient use of this ‘clock control’ is often cited as a key factor in successful teams.
If basketball can often be decided by which team scores last, does the `best’ team always win the championship? Are the most successful teams rewarded with spots in the playoffs? Given that the ultimate aim is to reach the playoffs and win the championship, in some ways the answer to the last two questions is always yes. En route to the NBA finals in the 2024-25 season, the Indiana Pacers won three games in the playoffs where they trailed going into the final minute. The eastern conference semifinal against the Cleveland Cavaliers was particularly notable; the Pacers trailed from midway through the first quarter before finally regaining the lead with one second left in the game. While many sports have such exciting last-gasp reversals, the high-scoring nature of basketball raises the question, how often do teams dominate scoring while losing games? This in turn brings up a larger question, is basketball ‘efficient’? Is there an inherent nature of the games and competition structure that rewards dominating games less than expected? To address these questions we will need both game and season data.

title: How Efficient is Basketball?
text:
Dominating Games & Last Minute Winners
Each basketball game generates a wealth of data, much of which is publicly accessible in recent years. Play-by-play game logs can be insightful as these record all distinct actions in a game, such as fouls or scoring events. From these game logs we can reconstruct any derived statistics on a per-game basis. Below is the scoring differential of that eastern conference semifinal between Indiana and Cleveland.









We can see that Cleveland were ahead for the vast majority of the game, after a short period of Indiana leading at the start. The deciding part however came with only three seconds to go, when the Pacers’ point guard Haliburton launched a successful 3-pt shot turning a 117-119 loss into a 120-199 win. While the result is obviously decided by the score at the end of play, Indiana were only leading for 7% of the total game time, compared to 88% for Cleveland (the remaining ~5% the score was even) so were the Pacers really the ‘better’ team? 88% is a lot of the game to lead and still lose. Do successful teams avoid what happened to Cleveland? Do they regularly come from behind as Indiana did?
To look into these questions we will use the game logs from the 2016-17 to the 2024-25 seasons. This covers 11,534 games in total, including 10755 regular season games. We will focus on the regular season games to ensure all teams have a comparable number of games in the dataset. To see how out of the ordinary Cleveland’s loss was, we calculate the fraction each team spends ahead/behind in a game, classifying these by whether they win or lose. Below we see the distribution of how long teams which lose have spent leading games. There is obviously a large peak at 0 for very one-sided games, but we can see a long tail all the way up to nearly 100% - the longest a team has lead the game and lost in this period is Clippers vs Wizards from January 2022, where the Clippers first took the lead with less than two seconds remaining. We can now see that Cleveland’s failure to complete a dominant win was unusual - only 79 games of the 10,740 analysed (15 games were dropped due to incomplete data) had a team who had longer in the lead, but went on to lose. That’s 0.74%, meaning this game would be in the top 1% of dominant losses.









The time spent behind in a win is the mirror of this distribution, as expected. The reverse measure, the time spent leading in games won shows a similar distribution, although the peak at 99% is smaller - it’s harder to dominate games than lose them comprehensively. Time spent in a tie is not counted in either statistic, so 0% time in front in a loss could include long stretches of tied game.









Using these distributions of data from the 9 seasons analysed we could label certain games according to their position in the distribution. We have labelled losses from the top 10 percentile of losing time in front as “dominant defeats”, which indicates that the losing team spent at least 61.5% of the game leading, while we also label wins from the bottom 10 percentile of winning time in front (also 61.5%) as “unlikely wins”. The plots below show each teams unlikely winds and dominant defeats across the 9 seasons. Comparing these to win percentage, we can see that generally more successful teams do have more unlikely wins (filled circles) than dominant defeats (open circles), although it is far from a distinct trend and the overall number of these games is comparable between teams and seasons.









We have seen that the extreme cases of dominant defeats and unlikely wins aren’t strong indicators of a teams success, but how do the measures that defined these games work out over a season? Do the teams that led for the longest in games have the highest win percentage? We can examine the correlations to find out.









The average winning time (averaged per season for each team) in front has a positive correlation with win percentage as expected, given that winning teams will spend longer in front. The standard deviation of the winning time in front has negative correlation with the win percentage, meaning that winning teams more consistently dominate games. The losing time in front also has a positive (but weaker) correlation with the win percentage, as winning teams will still hold the lead in games they have lost. Interestingly, the standard deviation of the losing time in front has a positive correlation with the win percentage, which is caused by more successful teams having more losses where they lead for significant periods.
The measures we have considered so far are all continuous measures, but the outcomes that a team desires are all binary outcomes - you either win the championship or you don’t, make the postseason or don’t. We can compare how well the continuous variables predict binary outcomes using a technique called Binomial Regression.

title: How Efficient is Basketball?
text:
Binomial Regression
Binomial Regression fits a logistic model (an S-shaped, sigmoidal curve) using the continuous explanatory variables to predict the binary response variable. This then yields a probability of the outcome for each value of the explanatory variable. We can see how this works using the win percentage to see how well this predicts the probability of a team making the postseason.









The points in this plot represent the final league win percentage of teams over the past 9 seasons, offset according to whether the team qualified for the postseason in that year. Points with a postseason prob at 1 made the postseason, while those at 0 missed out. Binomial Regression generates the grey curve which describes how we could predict a team’s postseason likelihood given its win percentage, based upon the previous seasons. The curve is fitted using two parameters; the ‘slope’ and the intercept. The intercept can be considered as the residual chance of making the playoffs when the team wins no games. In this case, the intercept is 2.4E-9, meaning a team winning no games has about a 1 in 400 million chance of making the postseason. The ‘slope’ is 1.5, which means that the odds ratio (given by p/(1-p)) of making the postseason increase by 1.5 for each percentage point increase in win percentage. We can also calculate that the tipping point at which making the postseason is more likely than not (i.e. 50% probability) is a 48% win percentage. A win percentage above 54% gives a 90% chance of making the postseason. We can also determine how unlikely the outliers we see in this data are - the highest win percentage not to make the postseason belongs to the ’18 Denver Nuggets with 56%. This would normally give a 96% chance of making the postseason, equal to 26 to 1 in favour! The ’22 Spurs made the postseason with a winning percentage of 41%, which would normally give them a 5% chance, or 19 to 1 against. Qualification for the postseason in basketball depends on a teams position within the division rather than win percentage only, and these statistics highlight how the divisional system can be a mixed bag.
Reaching the postseason is obviously not the only outcome teams strive for each year, the playoffs have multiple stages, so we should consider how well win percentage predicts these outcomes. We can also compare them to the new measure of game dominance that we have derived, the average winning/losing time in front.









As the teams progress further in the postseason, the model represented by the grey line is less confident in predicting success based upon the win percentage, which we can see as the logistic curve does not reach p=1 for the conference finals and beyond. A win percentage above 72% will give the team a 99% chance of making the conference semifinals, whereas a win percentage above 97% is required to give a similar level of confidence of a conference finals appearance. A win percentage above 77% is needed to give a ‘better than not’ (probability above 0.5) chance of making the NBA finals (above 78% is needed for the same level of confidence in an NBA title win). This has only been observed in six teams across the 9 years analysed, and three of those teams won the NBA title. Whereas each percentage point increase in win percentage increases a teams odds of making the postseason by 1.5, the odds of making the NBA finals only increase by 1.15. This means increasing the win percentage from 50% to 60% increases the odds of making the post season from 2 to 1 in favour to 133 to 1 in favour, but only shifts the odds of making the finals from 54 to 1 against to 12 to 1 against. At each stage we can use an ANOVA with a likelihood ratio test to determine if our model is appropriate for the data and significantly improves over the null hypotheses. All of the models used here meet this requirement.
We can replace win percentage with the average winning time in front to see how efficiently that works as a predictor of postseason success.









From the spread of data, we can see that the model will be less confident in predicting success based on the average winning time in front, as many teams who have been very dominant in their wins fail to make the postseason. This is also seen in the progression though the playoffs, with the models predicting much lower probabilities of success for the higher average winning time in front for the later stages. To have a 99% chance of making the postseason, the model suggests that a team should lead (on average) for 90% of the games in which it wins. This level of dominant wins has not been seen in the 9 years analysed here. To get over a 50% chance of making the conference semifinals, a team should lead on average for 76% of the games in which they win. All the models for later rounds of the playoffs require much higher, unachievable, levels of dominance in order for the model to suggest a greater than 50% chance. The losing time in front is a less accurate predictor of postseason success.

title: How Efficient is Basketball?
text:
Dominating But Not Winning = Inefficient?
Modelling with binomial regression shows that the win percentage of a team is a good predictor of reaching the postseason and a reasonable predictor of success within the postseason. This is to be expected, given that winning games is how a team achieves success. Analysis of the winning time in front shows that while it is correlated with win percentage, it is less effective at predicting how well a team will fair in the postseason. This is perhaps counter-intuitive, as we may expect that successful teams dominate games, spending the overwhelming majority of games in the lead, particularly given how frequent scoring is in basketball. Together this disconnect suggests that basketball is a very even sport, where even very successful teams will not be able to control most games, but rather ensure they win games by leading when it matters, at the end of the game. This does raise the possibility that basketball is not an efficient sport, where the teams who triumph at the end of the season are not necessarily the most dominant teams, although this unpredictability is often what fans relish in a sport.

title: The SPLit
text:
The Scottish Football League (SFL) is a professional football competition similar to other open European football leagues, featuring multiple divisions with promotion and relegation. The Scottish Premier League (SPL) is the top division. In the 2000/01 season, the SPL expanded from 10 to 12 teams (Lenten 2008). The addition of these teams had the potential to create fixture congestion as, traditionally, SPL teams played each other four times in a round-robin format, twice at home and twice away, with 36 fixtures played in total. With the new format, teams would have to complete 44 games.
To avoid fixture congestion and to make the total number of fixtures comparable to other top leagues in Europe, the SPL altered its tournament design. It “split” the season into two: the “Regular Season” and the “Play-offs”. During the Regular Season, teams play one another three times for a total of 33 matches. Then the league is “split” in two, creating two mini-leagues. Teams who finish in the top six places after 33 games play one another (one more time) in the “Championship Play-off” and the bottom six teams play one another in the “Relegation Play-off”. This leads to a total of 38 games being played by each team, the same number of matches as other European leagues (Reilly and Witt 2024).
The points accumulated prior to The Split are added to the points accrued after The Split. However, teams are bounded within their section of The Split. Therefore, after 33 games, if a team finishes in the top six, they cannot finish lower than sixth at the end of the season. Similarly, a team finishing in the bottom six after 33 games cannot finish higher than seventh after 38 games. As an example, the final 2023/24 SPL Table is displayed in Table 1, showing that ninth-placed Motherwell accrued more points than sixth-placed Dundee.

title: The SPLit
text:
Exploratory Data Analysis
In this section, we investigate the pattern of home attendance in the SPL (2023/24 season) using data from the football reference website.
Figure 1 shows home attendances as a proportion of stadium capacity for all 12 teams in the 2023/24 SPL season. Celtic, Rangers, and, to a lesser extent, Hearts, display stable attendance, nearly selling out all matches. In contrast, the other teams show fluctuating attendances.








Figure 1: Attendances as a proportion of stadium capacity for all teams in the 2023/24 SPL Season. Solid lines indicate teams in the Championship Play-off. Dashed lines indicate teams in the Relegation Play-off.




To investigate this further, home attendances for four SPL teams in 2023/24 (Celtic, Rangers, Dundee, and Aberdeen), each with different stadium capacities (60,500, 51,082, 11,850, and 21,412) are plotted in Figure 2.












(a) Celtic (Championship Play-off).












(b) Rangers (Championship Play-off).














(c) Dundee (Championship Play-off).












(d) Aberdeen (Relegation Play-off).







Figure 2: Home attendances for four example SPL Teams in the 2023/24 Season. The reported stadium capacity is shown as a horizontal dashed blue line. Blue background denotes play-off matches.



It appears that attendance fluctuations are driven by the opposition, with higher attendances when the “Old Firm” teams (or a historic rival) visit. In particular, matched attendances against the same opposition (Pre- and Post-Split) are very similar. Furthermore, note that the three Post-Split fixtures for Aberdeen (who finished seventh Pre-Split, just missing out on the Championship Play-off) are against two of the opponents that drew the lowest attendances Pre-Split.

title: The SPLit
text:
Shiny Application
We have also developed an open-access Shiny Application (SPLit) to complement this blog post. This app plots alternative versions of Figure 1 and Figure 2 for other teams and seasons. The user selects one of three example SPL seasons from the dataset and an SPL team, and the app creates two (interactive) plots: Attendance as a Proportion of Stadium Capacity for all teams (top panel) and Home Match Attendance for the selected team (bottom panel). These interactive plots mirror Figure 1 and Figure 2 , allowing users to explore other seasons or teams to verify our conclusions. The app also provides additional information (such as raw attendance numbers for every match).

title: The SPLit
text:
Conclusions
In this blog post, we have investigated the impact of the policy to split the Scottish Premier League (SPL) into two after 33 games for post-season play. In particular, whether this format reduced attendance for teams finishing in the lower half of the standings. Our analysis suggests that teams finishing in the Relegation Play-off may face an attendance drop compared to teams just qualifying for the Championship Play-off. Figure 1 and Figure 2 suggest that the opposition, particularly the two superstar clubs Rangers and Celtic, drive these attendance differences.

title: Super Bowl LX: Seattle Seahawks vs. New England Patriots
text:
On the 7\(^{th}\) of February 2026, I locked in a statistical prediction: the Seattle Seahawks would beat the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX with a 60.3% probability, with an expected score of SEA 24.9 – NE 23.4. Two independent models — a FiveThirtyEight-inspired Elo rating system and a historical Monte Carlo simulation — had converged on the same verdict from entirely different assumptions, which is about the strongest form of agreement in statistical modelling. The betting markets were more bullish, pricing Seattle at approximately 70% on a -4.5 point spread; ten percentage points separated the models from the market’s collective wisdom.
The game was played, and Seattle obtained a convincing 29-13 victory against the Patriots. This result is sweet vengeance for Seahawks fans after their last encounter with the Patriots in Super Bowl XLIX back in 2015, when Tom Brady led his team to victory from a 10 point defecit in the 4\(^{th}\) quarter, to win 28-24. If you haven’t seen that game, I do recommend it - many regard it as one of the best in NFL history. What makes Seattle’s win in this year’s Super Bowl so special is not only redemption for the franchise and a return to the biggest game in the sport, but also the hero arc of their quarterback, Sam Darnold. Darnold has had a tumultuous time in the NFL since joining in 2018. Seattle is the 5\(^{th}\) team in the league, and he has struggled to find form. However, his luck changed after joining the Minnesota Vikings, and he has had a stellar year since joining Seattle as a free agent in March 2025, throwing for over 4,000 yards and 25 touchdowns in the regular season. Having set the scene for Seattle’s historic win, it is now time to explore how the game unfolded and how accurate my predictions were.
It is relatively easy to make predictions; few have the desire to return and scrutinise them which is exactly what I will be doing. This article is the second half of my previous predictions about this game. We will examine not just whether Seattle won, but how - unpacking the play-by-play data to understand what drove the result, where the models were well-calibrated, and what the gaps between prediction and performance reveal about the limits of statistical forecasting in sport. It also gives us a chance to dig into which aspects won and lost the game for each team.






NotePrediction Accountability

title: Super Bowl LX: Seattle Seahawks vs. New England Patriots
text:
On the 7\(^{th}\) of February 2026, I locked in a statistical prediction: the Seattle Seahawks would beat the New England Patriots in Super Bowl LX with a 60.3% probability, with an expected score of SEA 24.9 – NE 23.4. Two independent models — a FiveThirtyEight-inspired Elo rating system and a historical Monte Carlo simulation — had converged on the same verdict from entirely different assumptions, which is about the strongest form of agreement in statistical modelling. The betting markets were more bullish, pricing Seattle at approximately 70% on a -4.5 point spread; ten percentage points separated the models from the market’s collective wisdom.
The game was played, and Seattle obtained a convincing 29-13 victory against the Patriots. This result is sweet vengeance for Seahawks fans after their last encounter with the Patriots in Super Bowl XLIX back in 2015, when Tom Brady led his team to victory from a 10 point defecit in the 4\(^{th}\) quarter, to win 28-24. If you haven’t seen that game, I do recommend it - many regard it as one of the best in NFL history. What makes Seattle’s win in this year’s Super Bowl so special is not only redemption for the franchise and a return to the biggest game in the sport, but also the hero arc of their quarterback, Sam Darnold. Darnold has had a tumultuous time in the NFL since joining in 2018. Seattle is the 5\(^{th}\) team in the league, and he has struggled to find form. However, his luck changed after joining the Minnesota Vikings, and he has had a stellar year since joining Seattle as a free agent in March 2025, throwing for over 4,000 yards and 25 touchdowns in the regular season. Having set the scene for Seattle’s historic win, it is now time to explore how the game unfolded and how accurate my predictions were.
It is relatively easy to make predictions; few have the desire to return and scrutinise them which is exactly what I will be doing. This article is the second half of my previous predictions about this game. We will examine not just whether Seattle won, but how - unpacking the play-by-play data to understand what drove the result, where the models were well-calibrated, and what the gaps between prediction and performance reveal about the limits of statistical forecasting in sport. It also gives us a chance to dig into which aspects won and lost the game for each team.
